title: Immigration concern is turning public systems into places of practical non-use for immigrant families
source_unit: Urban Institute, Immigrant Families Disengaged from Public Life and Essential Services Because of Immigration Concerns in 2025: Findings from the Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey
geography: United States; nationally representative Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, with analysis of adults in immigrant families and mixed-status families

observations.period: December 2025 survey; participation in essential activities

denominator.unit: adults in immigrant families analyzed from the WBNS

any_disengagement.unit: percent reporting that their family did not engage in an activity essential to well-being because of immigration concerns

work_nonuse.unit: percent reporting not going to work because of immigration concerns

healthcare_nonuse.unit: percent reporting not visiting a health-care setting because of immigration concerns

community_nonuse.unit: percent reporting not participating in religious services or community events because of immigration concerns

mechanism.value: Concern about immigration status can reduce practical use of work, care, mobility, and community infrastructure before any formal denial occurs

observations.method: Urban Institute analysis of the December 2025 Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, an annual nationally representative survey of adults monitoring family well-being and safety-net participation.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported associations measured at one survey round; the estimates do not establish which enforcement action caused each avoidance decision or whether non-use was temporary or durable.
observations.subgroup: Adults in immigrant families, including families with and without undocumented members; activities include work, driving, health care, school and child care, police contact, and community participation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some reported avoidance may reflect general uncertainty, misinformation, or unrelated barriers rather than direct enforcement exposure; concern could also prompt protective household planning or use of trusted intermediaries.

observations.period: December 2025 survey; mixed-status versus immigrant-family comparison

denominator.unit: adults in immigrant families, with subgroup comparison by presence of an undocumented family member

doctor_or_hospital_worry_mixed_status.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry about visiting a doctor, clinic, or hospital

doctor_or_hospital_worry_us_citizen_only.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry among immigrant families made up entirely of US citizens

work_worry_mixed_status.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry about going to work

work_worry_us_citizen_only_immigrant_fam.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry among immigrant families made up entirely of US citizens

police_contact_worry_mixed_status.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry about talking to police

police_contact_worry_us_citizen_only_imm.unit: percent reporting some or a lot of worry among immigrant families made up entirely of US citizens

mechanism.value: Legal-status heterogeneity within a household distributes the perceived risk of ordinary public contact across the whole family

observations.method: Weighted survey subgroup comparisons reported by the Urban Institute; estimates compare mixed-status families with immigrant families composed entirely of US citizens.
observations.uncertainty: The subgroup contrasts are not causal estimates and may reflect differences in legal status, local enforcement awareness, geography, family composition, or other unmeasured conditions.
observations.subgroup: Mixed-status immigrant families versus immigrant families whose members are all US citizens; the report also notes that concern is not confined to families with undocumented members.
observations.counterinterpretation: The presence of an undocumented member may proxy for other socioeconomic or administrative exposures; higher worry does not mean every family actually withdrew from the activity.

observations.period: December 2025 survey; safety-net participation and administrative trust

denominator.unit: adults in immigrant families analyzed from the WBNS

green_card_concern.unit: percent reporting that their family avoided safety-net programs because of concern about jeopardizing a family member's green-card eligibility

data_sharing_concern.unit: percent reporting that their family avoided safety-net programs because of concern that personal information would be shared with immigration authorities

programs.value: Examples include Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program

mechanism.value: Perceived data and eligibility risk can turn formal safety-net availability into non-take-up, shifting public capacity from support to surveillance in household decision-making

observations.method: Urban Institute survey analysis of reported family decisions to avoid safety-net programs because of immigration-related concerns.
observations.uncertainty: Avoidance is self-reported and the survey does not measure the amount of benefits forgone, later re-entry, actual data-sharing events, or the independent effect of formal public-charge rules.
observations.subgroup: Adults in immigrant families, including families with children and mixed-status households that may include US-citizen members eligible for services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some families may avoid programs because of confusion or generalized political fear even where legal eligibility and data protections remain; others may obtain support through community organizations or informal networks.

observations.period: 2017-2025 WBNS program; survey design and measurement boundary

denominator.unit: approximately adults surveyed in the expanded 2025 WBNS round; the analysis focuses on 2,234 adults in immigrant families

survey_continuity.value: The WBNS has been fielded annually since 2017

age_coverage.value: The 2025 round included adults ages 18 to 64 and an expanded sample of adults ages 65 and older

interpretive_scope.value: The evidence measures perceived risk, avoidance, and non-participation during an enforcement-intensive year; it does not measure the full local enforcement landscape or community-level economic effects

observations.method: Repeated annual nationally representative survey with a 2025 immigrant-family analytic sample; this record preserves the report's sampling and measurement boundary.
observations.uncertainty: Repeated cross-sectional survey design supports population estimates for the measured round but not individual trajectories, long-term adaptation, or causal effects of a particular policy.
observations.subgroup: Immigrant families, mixed-status families, families with children, and older adults included in the expanded 2025 survey frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: A single high-salience enforcement period may overstate durable withdrawal; subsequent institutional reassurance, legal clarification, or trusted intermediaries could change behavior.

related_sources.claim: Official downloadable brief with methodology and figures.
Preceding Urban Institute WBNS immigration-concern measurement from December 2024.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. route from immigration enforcement concern through household risk perception, practical non-use of work, health care, schools, police, community life, and safety-net programs, with disproportionate exposure in mixed-status families. It is nationally representative survey evidence for the measured 2025 round, not respondent-level longitudinal data, a causal estimate of enforcement effects, a complete account of local enforcement, or proof of durable institutional withdrawal.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Urban Institute publication page was reviewed for the WBNS sample, 2025 estimates, subgroup comparisons, safety-net avoidance, and repeated-survey methodology.
